summary.text: Take \(n=33085221781504=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009\), where \(4409\) and \(458009\) are distinct odd primes, and use \(a(n)=2\sigma(n)-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\), with both terms multiplicative on coprime factors. The factorwise evaluations give \(\sigma(n)=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010=66183576284700\) and \(\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011=132367152569399\), so \(a(n)=1\) although \(n\ne1,12\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\sigma(n)=\sum_{e\mid n}e
\]
denote the sum of the positive divisors of \(n\). The deficiency of a positive integer \(d\) is
\[
\delta(d)=2d-\sigma(d),
\]
and the sequence in question is therefore
\[
a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\delta(d)
    =\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr).
\]
We will exhibit a positive integer other than \(1\) and \(12\) for which this sum is \(1\).

Define the auxiliary function
\[
H(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d).
\]
Since the sum of the divisors \(d\) of \(n\) is itself \(\sigma(n)\), we immediately obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
 &=2\sum_{d\mid n}d-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\\
 &=2\sigma(n)-H(n). \tag{1}
\end{aligned}
\]

We will use the standard multiplicativity properties of these two functions. If \(r\) and \(s\) are coprime, every divisor of \(rs\) has a unique expression \(uv\), where \(u\mid r\) and \(v\mid s\). Consequently
\[
\sigma(rs)=\sum_{u\mid r,\,v\mid s}uv
          =\left(\sum_{u\mid r}u\right)
           \left(\sum_{v\mid s}v\right)
          =\sigma(r)\sigma(s). \tag{2}
\]
The same unique decomposition, together with (2), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(rs)
 &=\sum_{w\mid rs}\sigma(w)
   =\sum_{u\mid r,\,v\mid s}\sigma(uv)\\
 &=\sum_{u\mid r,\,v\mid s}\sigma(u)\sigma(v)
   =H(r)H(s). \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus both \(\sigma\) and \(H\) are multiplicative on coprime arguments.

Consider now
\[
N=33085221781504.
\]
Its factorization relevant to the calculation is
\[
N=16384\cdot 4409\cdot 458009
  =2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009. \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, \(4409\cdot458009=2019361681\), and multiplication by \(16384\) gives \(33085221781504\).

For completeness, the two odd factors in (4) are prime. Here is a finite primality certificate. We use the following elementary form of Lucas's criterion: if the complete prime factorization of \(m-1\) is known and there is an integer \(g\) such that
\[
g^{m-1}\equiv1\pmod m
\]
and, for every prime \(q\mid m-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(g^{(m-1)/q}-1,m\bigr)=1,
\]
then \(m\) is prime. To see why, let \(r\) be any prime divisor of \(m\). The displayed conditions imply that the order of \(g\) modulo \(r\) is divisible by every prime power occurring in \(m-1\), hence is \(m-1\). Since that order divides \(r-1\), one has \(m-1\mid r-1\), so \(r\ge m\). As \(r\mid m\), this forces \(r=m\), proving that \(m\) is prime.

Starting from the evident primality of \(2\), the following table supplies recursive certificates. In each row, the entry in the final column corresponding to a prime \(q\mid m-1\) is the residue
\(g^{(m-1)/q}\pmod m\). Direct repeated-squaring computations give \(g^{m-1}\equiv1\pmod m\) in every row, and the residue listed for each \(q\), minus \(1\), is coprime to \(m\).

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
m&m-1&g& q:\ g^{(m-1)/q}\bmod m\\ \hline
3&2&2&2:2\\
5&2^2&2&2:4\\
7&2\cdot3&3&2:6,\ 3:2\\
19&2\cdot3^2&2&2:18,\ 3:7\\
29&2^2\cdot7&2&2:28,\ 7:16\\
229&2^2\cdot3\cdot19&6&2:228,\ 3:134,\ 19:165\\
57251&2\cdot5^3\cdot229&2&2:57250,\ 5:55371,\ 229:48088\\
4409&2^3\cdot19\cdot29&3&2:4408,\ 19:209,\ 29:3965\\
458009&2^3\cdot57251&3&2:458008,\ 57251:6561
\end{array}
\]

For example, in the row for \(4409\), the three relevant gcds are
\(\gcd(4407,4409)\), \(\gcd(208,4409)\), and \(\gcd(3964,4409)\), all equal to \(1\); the other rows are checked in exactly the same way by the Euclidean algorithm. The factorizations in the second column are direct integer multiplications. Applying the criterion successively down the dependency chain proves that \(19\) and \(29\) are prime and hence that \(4409\) is prime; it also proves that \(229\), then \(57251\), and finally \(458009\) are prime.

The factors in (4) are therefore pairwise coprime: the two primes \(4409\) and \(458009\) are distinct and odd, so neither has a common factor with \(2^{14}\), and two distinct primes are coprime.

We next evaluate \(\sigma\) and \(H\) on each factor. For the power of two,
\[
\sigma(2^{14})=1+2+2^2+\cdots+2^{14}=2^{15}-1=32767. \tag{5}
\]
Moreover, the divisors of \(2^{14}\) are exactly \(2^i\) for \(0\le i\le14\), and
\(\sigma(2^i)=1+2+\cdots+2^i=2^{i+1}-1\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(2^{14})
 &=\sum_{i=0}^{14}\sigma(2^i)
   =\sum_{i=0}^{14}(2^{i+1}-1)\\
 &=(2+2^2+\cdots+2^{15})-15\\
 &=(2^{16}-2)-15
   =65519. \tag{6}
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(p\) is prime, its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(p\). Thus
\[
\sigma(p)=p+1
\]
and
\[
H(p)=\sigma(1)+\sigma(p)=1+(p+1)=p+2. \tag{7}
\]
Applying (7) to the two primes above gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
p&\sigma(p)&H(p)\\ \hline
4409&4410&4411\\
458009&458010&458011.
\end{array} \tag{8}
\]

Because the three factors in (4) are pairwise coprime, multiplicativity (2), together with (5) and (8), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma(N)
 &=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010\\
 &=144502470\cdot458010\\
 &=66183576284700. \tag{9}
\end{aligned}
\]
Similarly, by (3), (6), and (8),
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(N)
 &=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011\\
 &=289004309\cdot458011\\
 &=132367152569399. \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting (9) and (10) into identity (1), we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
 &=2\sigma(N)-H(N)\\
 &=2\cdot66183576284700-132367152569399\\
 &=132367152569400-132367152569399\\
 &=1.
\end{aligned}
\]

But
\[
N=33085221781504>12,
\]
so \(N\) is neither \(1\) nor \(12\). We have therefore found a positive integer \(N\notin\{1,12\}\) for which \(a(N)=1\). This contradicts the forward implication in the proposed biconditional
\[
a(n)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n=1\text{ or }n=12.
\]
Hence the conjecture is false.
